chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
title: George Tremblay and atonal writing
summary: Mandel praises George Tremblay, who taught many film writers a sensual Berg-like approach to atonality.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: You mentioned with George Tremblay, we might as well talk about that now it might be getting a little ahead of ourselves but not really. As I recall a number of prominent film writers have studied with him, is that…

David Raksin did. Oh, he’s wonderful, he was wonderful and he understood a lot, he understood about jazz, he understood about all types of music, even though he was strictly a classicist himself he was not all in the tradition. And he wrote gorgeous music that was atonal but tonal, you know it was sort of an Alban Berg type of approach to atonality, using rows, but it was very sensual music like Berg’s was, or is.
So you basically delved into atonal writing with him as well then?
How much has come out in your own writing of that do you think?
It's hard for me to be objective about that, I don’t know, you never know what comes out from what you may have rubbed off in different places. I really can't say, I don’t know.
